title: ML: data contracts and deployment decisions
summary: Twelve practical contracts for point-in-time data, a boosted model, drift, conformal intervals, importance, threshold costs, cohort metrics, artifact identity and bounded serving. Small local experiments make operational assumptions explicit.

lessons.title: Validate the serving feature contract
lessons.body:
# Validate the serving feature contract

Training and serving must agree on both feature meaning and feature order. A dictionary with the right values in the wrong matrix columns can produce plausible but incorrect predictions. Validate the schema at the boundary and construct columns from the declared order.

This contract rejects missing, extra, boolean and nonfinite values. The model should not silently replace invalid inputs with zeros. Real schemas also need units, availability timestamps and categorical vocabularies. A numeric shape check is only one layer of a reproducible preprocessing contract.

```python
schema=["age","count"]
row={"count":4,"age":20}
print([row[name] for name in schema])
```

## Review the design

The schema order is part of model identity. Version it with the preprocessing state and weights, and reject unsupported schema versions at serving rather than guessing a column mapping.
lessons.task: Implement feature_matrix(rows,schema). Require unique schema names and exact row keys; each value is int or float, not bool, and finite. Return float rows in schema order, without mutating input.

checks.name: rejects missing extra and nonfinite data
booleans and duplicate features fail

hints: Validate exact keys before constructing any column list.
Use the schema sequence for ordering and reject bool separately from int.
The schema order is part of model identity. Version it with the preprocessing state and weights, and reject unsupported schema versions at serving rather than guessing a column mapping.
lessons.explanation: The schema order is part of model identity. Version it with the preprocessing state and weights, and reject unsupported schema versions at serving rather than guessing a column mapping.

lessons.title: Join only features available at prediction time
lessons.body:
# Join only features available at prediction time

A historical event timestamp does not prove that its feature value was available to a prediction system then. Late ingestion and backfilled corrections can leak future knowledge into training. A point-in-time join must consider publication or availability time as well as event time.

This exercise chooses the latest eligible event per entity for each query. Both timestamps must be no later than the prediction timestamp. Ties are resolved by availability time. Missing history returns None instead of borrowing a future observation. Real pipelines must also document revisions and retention of historical feature versions.

```python
events=[(1,2,"known"),(2,8,"late")]
prediction_time=4
print([v for event,available,v in events if event<=prediction_time and available<=prediction_time])
```

## Review the design

Point-in-time correctness is a data-lineage property, not just a split choice. Backfills should preserve availability history so offline experiments can reconstruct what the online system actually knew.
lessons.task: Implement asof_values(events,queries). Events are (entity,event_time,available_time,value); queries are (entity,time). Return latest eligible value ordered by (event_time,available_time), or None. No mutation; ties with identical timestamp pairs are outside this contract.

checks.name: entities and missing history stay isolated
event and publication order both matter

hints: Filter by entity, event time and availability time before selecting a maximum.
A later publication of an older event does not outrank a newer eligible event.

Point-in-time correctness is a data-lineage property, not just a split choice. Backfills should preserve availability history so offline experiments can reconstruct what the online system actually knew.
lessons.explanation: Point-in-time correctness is a data-lineage property, not just a split choice. Backfills should preserve availability history so offline experiments can reconstruct what the online system actually knew.

lessons.title: Fit residual trees in a tiny gradient-boosted regressor
lessons.body:
# Fit residual trees in a tiny gradient-boosted regressor

Gradient boosting adds weak models that reduce the current residual error. For squared loss, fitting each new stump to target minus current prediction follows the negative gradient direction. Shrinkage scales each update and changes how many rounds are useful.

The exercise fits one-dimensional decision stumps by exhaustive split search. This is a real local training algorithm, with a constant baseline and reproducible tie handling, not a wrapper around supplied predictions. It intentionally omits large-scale histogram algorithms, missing-value routing and early stopping. Select rounds and learning rate on validation data, never by improving final test error.

```python
target=[0.,0.,2.,2.]
base=sum(target)/len(target)
residual=[y-base for y in target]
print(base,residual)
```

## Review the design

A trainable baseline makes every later gain measurable. This tiny learner demonstrates gradient boosting correctly, while production libraries add numerical, categorical, performance and distributed engineering that must be evaluated separately.
lessons.task: Implement fit_boost(x,y,rounds,rate) and predict_boost(model,x). Fit a mean baseline, then squared-error optimal residual stumps at midpoints of distinct x; ties choose smallest cut. Model is dict base, rate, stumps (cut,left,right). Constant x uses a constant residual stump with cut=inf. Validate nonempty equal finite data, rounds>=0 integer, 0<rate<=1.

checks.name: baseline constant feature and invalid input

hints: Fit each stump to the current residuals, not to the original targets.
Update every training prediction with rate times the chosen residual stump.

A trainable baseline makes every later gain measurable. This tiny learner demonstrates gradient boosting correctly, while production libraries add numerical, categorical, performance and distributed engineering that must be evaluated separately.
lessons.explanation: A trainable baseline makes every later gain measurable. This tiny learner demonstrates gradient boosting correctly, while production libraries add numerical, categorical, performance and distributed engineering that must be evaluated separately.

lessons.title: Measure binned drift with smoothing and fixed boundaries
lessons.body:
# Measure binned drift with smoothing and fixed boundaries

Population stability index compares the proportions in fixed reference bins with those observed later. Zero occupancy makes logarithms undefined, so a declared smoothing convention is part of the calculation. Fit bin boundaries on reference data before observing the monitoring window.

Drift is not the same as model performance degradation. A feature distribution may shift harmlessly, while labels or conditional relationships shift without a large PSI. Report sample sizes, bin definitions and relevant slices. This exercise receives bin counts directly so it tests the monitoring arithmetic without pretending to detect every kind of dataset change.

```python
import math
reference=[.5,.5];current=[.25,.75]
print(sum((b-a)*math.log(b/a) for a,b in zip(reference,current)))
```

## Review the design

Smoothing reduces instability but changes the estimate, especially on tiny windows. PSI thresholds are not universal laws; calibrate alerts against reference variation and observed model outcomes.
lessons.task: Implement psi(reference,current,epsilon=1e-6) for equal nonempty nonnegative finite bin counts with positive totals. Add epsilon to every bin count before normalizing each histogram; return sum((q-p)*log(q/p)). Require finite epsilon>0.

checks.name: zero bins remain finite and shifted bins positive
invalid monitoring windows fail

hints: Normalize smoothed counts separately for the two windows.
Never evaluate log of a zero probability.
Smoothing reduces instability but changes the estimate, especially on tiny windows. PSI thresholds are not universal laws; calibrate alerts against reference variation and observed model outcomes.
lessons.explanation: Smoothing reduces instability but changes the estimate, especially on tiny windows. PSI thresholds are not universal laws; calibrate alerts against reference variation and observed model outcomes.

lessons.title: Use a symmetric distribution divergence
lessons.body:
# Use a symmetric distribution divergence

Jensen-Shannon divergence compares two distributions through their midpoint. It is symmetric and remains finite for disjoint support, unlike a one-way KL divergence with a zero denominator. The logarithm base determines the scale; this exercise uses natural logs.

A value near zero means similar marginal proportions, not identical joint behavior or stable model quality. Counts must share the same bin vocabulary. Empty or negative histograms are invalid observations, rather than another form of drift. Keep feature construction and bin definitions versioned with the monitoring configuration.

```python
import math
p=[1.,0.];q=[0.,1.];m=[.5,.5]
print(sum(x*math.log(x/y) for x,y in zip(p,m) if x))
```

## Review the design

Natural-log Jensen-Shannon divergence lies between zero and log(2). The metric compares the supplied bins, so missing a critical slice or dependency can still hide a production problem.
lessons.task: Implement js_divergence(a,b), normalizing equal nonempty nonnegative finite count arrays with positive totals. Compute half KL(p||m)+half KL(q||m), skipping zero numerator terms.

checks.name: invalid data is not a drift score

hints: Create normalized p, q and their midpoint m.
A zero numerator contributes zero; it does not require evaluating a logarithm.
Natural-log Jensen-Shannon divergence lies between zero and log(2). The metric compares the supplied bins, so missing a critical slice or dependency can still hide a production problem.
lessons.explanation: Natural-log Jensen-Shannon divergence lies between zero and log(2). The metric compares the supplied bins, so missing a critical slice or dependency can still hide a production problem.

lessons.title: Use the finite-sample conformal rank
lessons.body:
# Use the finite-sample conformal rank

Split conformal regression calibrates an interval width using held-out absolute residuals. The finite-sample rank is ceil((n+1)(1-alpha)), not an ordinary interpolated percentile. If that rank exceeds the available calibration sample, the conservative interval is unbounded.

Coverage is marginal under exchangeability between calibration and future observations. It does not guarantee conditional coverage for every subgroup or survive arbitrary time drift. The calibration residuals must come from a model that was not fitted on those calibration outcomes. Keep the final test set separate from choosing the score or calibration strategy.

```python
import math
n=9;alpha=.1
print(math.ceil((n+1)*(1-alpha)))
```

## Review the design

The guarantee depends on exchangeable calibration and future scores. An infinite interval honestly reports insufficient calibration information at the requested error level rather than silently overstating confidence.
lessons.task: Implement conformal_radius(residuals,alpha) with finite nonnegative residuals, nonempty input and 0<alpha<1. Return sorted residual at one-based rank ceil((n+1)*(1-alpha)); return inf if rank>n.

checks.name: invalid residuals or coverage fail

hints: Calculate the one-based rank with n+1, then convert it to a list index.
Do not clamp an unavailable rank to n and claim the same guarantee.

The guarantee depends on exchangeable calibration and future scores. An infinite interval honestly reports insufficient calibration information at the requested error level rather than silently overstating confidence.
lessons.explanation: The guarantee depends on exchangeable calibration and future scores. An infinite interval honestly reports insufficient calibration information at the requested error level rather than silently overstating confidence.

lessons.title: Measure reliance on a feature using held-out loss
lessons.body:
# Measure reliance on a feature using held-out loss

A feature can be strongly associated with an outcome without a trained model relying on it. Permutation importance measures the change in held-out loss when one feature's alignment with the outcomes is disrupted. It evaluates the particular fitted model and test population.

This exercise uses a deterministic one-position rotation as an inspectable perturbation. It is one reference experiment, not a full estimate with repeated random permutations and uncertainty. Correlated features may substitute for each other, so low importance does not establish irrelevance or causality. Never refit the model on the perturbed evaluation data.

```python
rows=[[1,10],[2,20],[3,30]]
rotated=[r[:] for r in rows]
column=[r[0] for r in rows]
for i,row in enumerate(rotated):row[0]=column[(i+1)%3]
print(rows,rotated)
```

## Review the design

The measured loss difference is predictive reliance under a specific perturbation, not a causal feature effect. Use repeated held-out permutations and uncertainty estimates for a serious interpretation.
lessons.task: Implement rotated_importance(predict,rows,targets,column). Return perturbed MSE minus baseline MSE, rotating the chosen column by one row. Require nonempty matching row/target counts and a valid column in every row. Do not mutate rows.

lessons.title: Select an operating threshold using explicit error costs
lessons.body:
# Select an operating threshold using explicit error costs

A classifier's best operating threshold depends on the costs of false positives and false negatives, not on a universal value of one half. Choose the threshold on validation data after probability or ranking training has finished, then lock it before final testing.

This exercise evaluates a supplied candidate set and returns total cost. It deliberately uses a deterministic higher-threshold tie break. Real deployments should include capacity constraints, subgroup behavior and changes in prevalence. A threshold that minimizes historical validation cost can still fail when the outcome distribution or downstream cost changes.

```python
labels=[0,1]
scores=[.6,.7]
threshold=.5
false_positives=sum(y==0 and s>=threshold for y,s in zip(labels,scores))
print(false_positives)
```

## Review the design

Threshold tuning is part of model selection. Its validation data must not be reused as a supposedly untouched test set, and cost assumptions should be documented and monitored.
lessons.task: Implement cost_threshold(labels,scores,candidates,fp_cost,fn_cost). Predict 1 at score>=threshold. Return (threshold,total_cost), minimizing cost and choosing the higher threshold on ties. Validate nonempty equal data, binary labels, finite scores/candidates and finite nonnegative costs.

checks.name: invalid input is rejected

hints: Count false positives and false negatives separately at each candidate threshold.
Minimize the pair (cost,-threshold) for the declared tie rule.
Threshold tuning is part of model selection. Its validation data must not be reused as a supposedly untouched test set, and cost assumptions should be documented and monitored.
lessons.explanation: Threshold tuning is part of model selection. Its validation data must not be reused as a supposedly untouched test set, and cost assumptions should be documented and monitored.

lessons.title: Keep small cohorts visible without overclaiming their scores
lessons.body:
# Keep small cohorts visible without overclaiming their scores

An aggregate score can improve while a cohort becomes substantially worse. A deployment report should retain both cohort counts and error measurements so a reviewer can see how much evidence supports each number. Hiding small cohorts entirely can hide an important coverage problem.

This exercise reports mean absolute error for every named cohort and marks whether it reaches a required count. That count is a reporting threshold, not a statistical guarantee. Compare confidence and missingness before making a release decision, and define cohorts before inspecting results to reduce selective reporting.

```python
groups=["new","new","returning"]
errors=[1.,3.,10.]
print({g:sum(e for k,e in zip(groups,errors) if k==g) for g in set(groups)})
```

## Review the design

A sample-count flag does not establish fairness, causality or sufficient power. The report is evidence for a review, and the choice of metric, cohort and acceptable harm needs a separate domain-specific decision.
lessons.task: Implement cohort_mae(groups,truth,predicted,min_count). Return dict group->{n,mae,supported}. Require equal nonempty lengths, positive integer min_count and finite truth/predictions. supported means n>=min_count.

checks.name: invalid evidence is rejected

hints: Group absolute residuals while preserving their sample counts.
Keep unsupported cohorts in the report with an explicit supported flag.

A sample-count flag does not establish fairness, causality or sufficient power. The report is evidence for a review, and the choice of metric, cohort and acceptable harm needs a separate domain-specific decision.
lessons.explanation: A sample-count flag does not establish fairness, causality or sufficient power. The report is evidence for a review, and the choice of metric, cohort and acceptable harm needs a separate domain-specific decision.

lessons.title: Bind model bytes to ordered features and preprocessing
lessons.body:
# Bind model bytes to ordered features and preprocessing

A weights file alone does not identify a reproducible predictor. Feature order, preprocessing version and schema determine how those weights are used. Compute an artifact identifier from a canonical metadata representation and a digest of the exact weight bytes.

Dictionary key ordering should not change identity, but changing feature order must change it. This is content identity, not proof of who produced an artifact. A trusted registry or authenticated signature supplies provenance. Do not load arbitrary serialized Python objects merely because their bytes have a matching locally supplied hash.

```python
import hashlib,json
metadata={"features":["a","b"],"pipeline":"v1"}
encoded=json.dumps(metadata,sort_keys=True,separators=(",",":")).encode()
print(hashlib.sha256(encoded).hexdigest()[:12])
```

## Review the design

Content addressing detects changes only relative to a trusted expected identifier. It is not authentication, and it cannot make an unsafe deserialization format safe.
lessons.task: Implement model_identity(weights,features,pipeline) returning SHA256 hex of canonical UTF-8 JSON {weights_sha256,features,pipeline}, sort_keys=True,separators=(",",":"),ensure_ascii=False. Feature order matters; require distinct feature names.

checks.name: duplicate features are invalid

hints: Hash the bytes first, then include that digest in canonical metadata.
Keep the feature list ordered even though metadata dictionary keys are sorted.
Content addressing detects changes only relative to a trusted expected identifier. It is not authentication, and it cannot make an unsafe deserialization format safe.
lessons.explanation: Content addressing detects changes only relative to a trusted expected identifier. It is not authentication, and it cannot make an unsafe deserialization format safe.

lessons.title: Require quality, latency and cost evidence together
lessons.body:
# Require quality, latency and cost evidence together

A candidate model can improve an offline metric while exceeding the serving latency or cost budget. A release gate should evaluate all declared constraints and retain the reason for each rejection. Missing or nonfinite evidence should not be treated as a passing score.

This exercise is a deterministic policy over already collected evidence. It does not claim to perform a real deployment or statistical significance test. The quality margin and budgets are predeclared inputs. Production rollout additionally needs a shadow or canary phase, monitoring, rollback ownership and a plan for delayed outcome labels.

```python
candidate={"gain":.02,"p95_ms":80,"cost":.01}
print(candidate["gain"]>=.01 and candidate["p95_ms"]<=100)
```

## Review the design

The gate evaluates declared measurements, not their trustworthiness or sampling uncertainty. A serious release review also needs data lineage, confidence, slice performance and a rollback plan.
lessons.task: Implement promotion_reasons(candidate,min_gain,max_p95,max_cost). candidate has gain,p95_ms,cost. Return ordered reasons quality,latency,cost for failed bounds; missing/nonfinite evidence yields only ["invalid evidence"]. Require nonnegative latency and cost evidence.

checks.name: missing or invalid evidence never passes

hints: Validate evidence before comparing thresholds.
Accumulate every failed policy constraint in the specified order.
The gate evaluates declared measurements, not their trustworthiness or sampling uncertainty. A serious release review also needs data lineage, confidence, slice performance and a rollback plan.
lessons.explanation: The gate evaluates declared measurements, not their trustworthiness or sampling uncertainty. A serious release review also needs data lineage, confidence, slice performance and a rollback plan.

lessons.title: Pack inference requests within a declared memory budget
lessons.body:
# Pack inference requests within a declared memory budget

Inference throughput can improve with batching, but total batch size is constrained by memory and latency. A serving scheduler must define which request costs count against its budget and how oversized requests are handled. Silent overcommit can turn one large request into a service-wide failure.

This exercise uses declared byte costs and a first-fit-in-order sequential packing policy. It does not estimate GPU memory from token counts or claim to measure a real accelerator. Model weights, temporary activations and allocator overhead require separate budgets. Preserving request order makes the policy easy to replay and test.

```python
sizes=[4,3,5]
capacity=7
print(sum(sizes[:2])<=capacity)
print(sum(sizes)>capacity)
```

## Review the design

Admission by declared cost is an executable scheduling policy. Real serving needs measured memory headroom, deadline-aware admission and fairness across request classes; the arithmetic alone does not provide those guarantees.
lessons.task: Implement budget_batches(sizes,capacity), preserving order and packing consecutive positive integer sizes until the next would exceed positive integer capacity. Reject any individual size>capacity. Return lists of original indices.

checks.name: oversized and invalid requests fail

hints: Flush the current batch before adding a request that would exceed capacity.
Keep original indices so outputs can be matched to callers.

Admission by declared cost is an executable scheduling policy. Real serving needs measured memory headroom, deadline-aware admission and fairness across request classes; the arithmetic alone does not provide those guarantees.
